pages.x: Ethiopia was one of only two African countries never to have been colonised, and Italy had a score to settle: in 1896 Emperor Menelik II had crushed an Italian army at Adwa. In December 1934 a clash at the oasis of Walwal, on the border with Italian Somaliland, gave Mussolini an excuse.

Mussolini dreamed of a new Roman empire, and of avenging Adwa. He gathered a vast army in Eritrea and Somaliland, and on 3 October 1935, without declaring war, it crossed the border. Adwa fell within three days, and Italians celebrated their revenge.

Emperor Haile Selassie had begun to modernise his country, and had brought it into the League of Nations. His armies were brave, but many soldiers carried old rifles, or spears and swords, and he had only a handful of aircraft. He appealed to the League to defend a member under attack.

The League did condemn Italy, and banned trade in arms and many goods. But oil, which Italy's army needed most, was left off the list, and Britain let Italian ships carry troops through the Suez Canal. In December the British and French foreign ministers were caught planning to hand Mussolini much of Ethiopia.

The new Italian commander, Pietro Badoglio, used massed artillery, bombers, and mustard gas, banned by a treaty Italy had signed, sprayed from planes on soldiers and villages alike. Ethiopian armies were destroyed in the north, at Amba Aradam, Tembien and Maychew, where the emperor himself led the last attack.
pages.of: burned, blinded or killed by mustard gas

pages.x: On 2 May 1936 Haile Selassie left his capital by train for exile. Three days later Badoglio's motor columns drove into Addis Ababa, and Mussolini told a cheering crowd in Rome that Italy had an empire at last. The king of Italy took the title emperor of Ethiopia.

In June 1936 the exiled emperor spoke to the League of Nations in Geneva, while Italian journalists jeered. He warned the nations that what had been done to Ethiopia could be done to them: "It is us today. It will be you tomorrow." Within weeks the League dropped its sanctions.

Ethiopians fought on as guerrillas, the Patriots. After an attempt to kill the viceroy, Rodolfo Graziani, in Addis Ababa in February 1937, Italian soldiers, Blackshirts and civilians massacred people in the city for three days, and months later hundreds of monks were shot at the monastery of Debre Libanos.
pages.of: killed in Addis Ababa in three days

pages.x: Italy's empire in Ethiopia lasted five years: in 1941 British and Ethiopian forces drove the Italians out, and Haile Selassie rode back into his capital. The League of Nations never recovered from failing Ethiopia, and across Africa and the Caribbean the war made Ethiopia a symbol of freedom.
pts: Mustard gas was used on soldiers and civilians
The League of Nations failed to stop it
